title: Elastic cloud infrastructure from S3/EC2 to normalized on-demand pooled compute
pressure: Provisioning and operating scalable infrastructure imposed high fixed cost, delay and specialized operational burden on teams that primarily wanted to build applications.
preExistingWorldModel: Large internet companies already operated internal distributed storage and compute infrastructure; virtualization and web-service interfaces were available but not yet normalized as general on-demand infrastructure.
candidateRoutes: expose scalable storage/compute as metered web services
observationsAndInstruments: Amazon S3 launched in March 2006 exposing Amazon-scale storage through a web-service interface.
EC2 beta followed in August 2006 with resizable compute capacity obtainable within minutes and pay-for-use economics.
NIST later stabilized a technology-neutral definition around on-demand self-service, pooled configurable resources, rapid elasticity and measured service.
decisiveTests: can an external developer obtain storage/compute without owning the underlying datacenter
can capacity scale up/down on demand
can service boundaries preserve enough control while hiding physical infrastructure management
technicalOrScientificTransition: Internal infrastructure operating capability was projected through stable service interfaces into externally consumable, elastic capability.
rivalsAndFailures: Traditional hosting and private infrastructure remained useful under different control/compliance needs.
A web-service label alone was not sufficient; elasticity, pooling and measured service became important discriminators.
diffusionAndScaling: Small and large external consumers could increasingly access infrastructure scale previously associated with large operators.
standardsAndInstitutions: AWS owned service operation; NIST supplied a later common reference vocabulary rather than operational authority over providers.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Outsourcing infrastructure shifts rather than eliminates dependency, security, locality and provider-governance risks.
secondOrderEffects: Lower infrastructure acquisition latency changed the feasible experiment/startup/application space and enabled further platform/service layers.
sourceNativeSummary: Cloud infrastructure emerged by exposing proven large-scale storage/compute through low-friction, elastic, metered interfaces; later standardization clarified the capability without creating it.
